title: Music & Bands
tagline: The songs everyone knows, and the stories behind them.
description: Music is the easiest bridge between strangers. Learn a few great stories about famous bands, share Nepali music with pride, and handle karaoke, bad guitar and 'what music do you like?' with style.

vibe.scenario: The band plays a song you don't know. A traveller shouts, "Do you know this one?"

options.text: No idea, but I've already decided it's my favourite. Who is it?
Yes, of course, everyone knows this one, it's very famous, I love it, it's a classic song.
No.

vibe.why: Not knowing is fine. Turning it into curiosity gives them the fun of telling you.

vibe.scenario: A traveller asks, "What kind of music do you like?"

options.text: Everything.
Depends on the bus ride. Nepali folk for the mountains, old rock for the traffic, and Bollywood when nobody's watching.
Only good music, not the stuff you probably listen to.

vibe.why: "Everything" says nothing. A few specific, funny details give them five things to ask about.

vibe.scenario: A traveller is playing guitar — enthusiastically, and a little out of tune.

options.text: You're a bit out of tune, you know. The G string is flat — I can hear it from here.
Nice guitar.
Don't stop — everyone's pretending not to listen, which means they love it. Know any Nepali songs?

vibe.why: Music in a hostel is about the mood, not perfection. Encouragement plus a request makes you part of it.

vibe.scenario: A friend grabs your phone: "Your music taste is terrible."

options.text: It's not terrible.
It's not terrible, it's ahead of its time. Give it twenty years.
Your taste is worse.

vibe.why: A confident, silly defence keeps the banter going. Hitting back just makes it a contest.

vibe.scenario: The travellers ask you to sing a Nepali song. You're shy.

options.text: Why do you want to hear it? You won't understand the words anyway.
Only if you sing one from your country after. Deal? (Then sing the first line of "Resham Firiri".)
No, no, I can't sing.

vibe.why: A trade makes it fair and fun. Everyone is a little embarrassed together, and that's how friendships start.

vibe.scenario: You just sang very badly. Everyone is laughing.

options.text: Thank you, thank you. I'm here all week. Please don't come back.
Stop laughing! It's not funny!
Sorry, I'm really bad at singing, I don't know why I did that, sorry everyone.

vibe.why: Acting like a proud star after a terrible song is the funniest possible ending.

vibe.scenario: A traveller says their favourite band is one you've never heard of.

options.text: They can't be that good if I've never heard of them.
I don't know them.
Never heard of them — so you're my music teacher now. Play me the one song I have to know.

vibe.why: People love sharing music they love. Asking for "the one song" gives them a lovely moment to share.

vibe.scenario: A traveller plays a song on their phone. They go quiet. It clearly means something to them.

options.text: (Let the song finish. Then, softly:) That one means something to you, doesn't it?
Ugh, this is so sad. Can we change it to something happy? This is making me sleepy.
Nice song.

vibe.why: Some songs carry memories. Waiting and asking gently can open the best conversation of the trip.

yesAnd.prompt: I'm going to a concert in Kathmandu next week.

cards.text: Who's playing? And will I fit in your suitcase?
cards.why: A real question and a joke.

cards.text: Then you're dangerous in a hostel at 6 a.m. What got you started?
cards.why: A tease and a question about their story.

cards.text: Then the floor is yours. I'll be your backing dancer.
cards.why: Joins their joy and makes it a moment.

yesAnd.prompt: I've never heard any Nepali music.

cards.why: Vague, and it sounds like a warning.

cards.text: Then I'm your DJ tonight. Three songs, and you tell me which one wins.
cards.why: Turns it into a game you play together.

yesAnd.prompt: I only listen to old music.

cards.text: Old like the Beatles, or old like your dad's car stereo? Give me your top three.
cards.why: A funny choice and an easy request.

yesAnd.prompt: Music festivals are my favourite thing.

cards.text: Best festival you've ever been to, and your worst moment there. Go.
cards.why: Best and worst questions always get stories.

dropIn.fact: Queen's "Bohemian Rhapsody" (1975) is almost six minutes long and has no repeating chorus — yet it became one of the most famous songs ever.
dropIn.prompt: At karaoke, a British traveller starts singing "Is this the real life?" and the whole bar joins in.

options.text: Six minutes, no chorus, and the whole bar still knows every word. That's Queen.
options.why: The fact arrives as admiration, in the middle of the fun.

options.text: "Bohemian Rhapsody" is almost six minutes long and has no repeating chorus, which was very unusual for a hit single in 1975.
options.why: Interesting, but you're lecturing during karaoke.

options.text: This song is too long.
options.why: Spoils everyone's favourite moment.

dropIn.fact: Freddie Mercury was born Farrokh Bulsara in Zanzibar and went to school in India.
dropIn.prompt: A traveller is wearing a Queen T-shirt.

options.text: Queen is old music.
options.why: Dismisses something they love.

options.text: Great shirt. Did you know Freddie Mercury went to school in India? So he's basically our neighbour.
options.why: A compliment plus a surprising local connection.

options.text: Freddie Mercury was born in Zanzibar and went to school in India, and his real name was Farrokh Bulsara.
options.why: Three facts in a row, no conversation.

dropIn.fact: In 1968 the Beatles travelled to Rishikesh, India, to study meditation, and wrote many songs there, lots of which ended up on the "White Album".
dropIn.prompt: A traveller doing a yoga course says, "I came to Asia to find myself."

options.text: Everyone says that.
options.why: Cynical, and it shuts them down.

options.text: The Beatles went to Rishikesh in 1968 to study meditation.
options.why: Related, but it misses them.

options.text: You're in good company — the Beatles came to India in 1968 to find themselves too, and went home with a pile of songs. What will you take home?
options.why: Links their journey to a legend and asks about them.

dropIn.fact: Bob Marley, from Jamaica, died in 1981 at just 36, but his songs are still played all over the world.
dropIn.prompt: The hostel has played "Three Little Birds" four times today. A traveller laughs about it.

options.text: Every hostel on Earth plays Bob Marley. He only lived to 36, and he's still the soundtrack of every backpacker alive.
options.why: Shared joke, then a fact that adds a little wonder.

options.text: Reggae is boring.
options.why: An opinion that kills the laugh.

options.text: Bob Marley died in 1981 when he was only 36 years old, but his music is still very popular around the world today.
options.why: Accurate, but it drops the joke they started.

dropIn.fact: ABBA won the Eurovision Song Contest in 1974 with "Waterloo", and went on to become one of the best-selling bands in history.
dropIn.prompt: A traveller tells you she's from Sweden.

options.text: Sweden won Eurovision in 1974 with ABBA.
options.why: Correct, a bit quiz-show.

options.text: Sweden! The country that won Eurovision with "Waterloo" and gave the world ABBA. Be honest — do you know every word of "Dancing Queen"?
options.why: Proud-of-you energy, then a question she'll laugh at.

options.text: ABBA is for old people.
options.why: Insults her country's pride and joy.

dropIn.fact: In 2016 Bob Dylan won the Nobel Prize in Literature for his song lyrics.
dropIn.prompt: A traveller says, "Song lyrics aren't real poetry."

options.text: Tell that to the Nobel committee — they gave Bob Dylan the Literature prize in 2016. What's the last lyric that really hit you?
options.why: Playful disagreement with proof, then a personal question.

options.text: Yes, you're right.
options.why: Gives up a great argument.

options.text: Bob Dylan won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2016, so some people think lyrics are poetry.
options.why: The point is there, but the fun isn't.

dropIn.fact: Taylor Swift's Eras Tour (2023–2024) became the highest-grossing concert tour in history, earning over two billion dollars.
dropIn.prompt: An American traveller admits, "I spent a crazy amount on Eras Tour tickets."

options.text: That's a waste of money.
options.why: Judging their joy.

options.text: Then you helped make history — it was the first tour to earn over two billion dollars. Worth it? Which era are you?
options.why: Makes their spending part of history, then a fan question.

options.text: The Eras Tour made over two billion dollars.
options.why: A number, not a conversation.

dropIn.fact: Michael Jackson's "Thriller" (1982) is the best-selling album of all time.
dropIn.prompt: At a party, someone starts doing the Thriller zombie dance.

options.text: Respect — best-selling album in history, and you still have the moves. Teach me the zombie part?
options.why: Praise, the fact, and an invitation to join.

options.text: "Thriller" is the best-selling album of all time, according to Guinness World Records.
options.why: True, but you're standing still while they dance.

options.text: That's so old.
options.why: A buzzkill.

dropIn.fact: Oasis reunited in 2025 for their first concerts since splitting up in 2009. The Live '25 tour sold nearly three million tickets across 41 shows.
dropIn.prompt: A traveller from Manchester says, "I saw the Oasis reunion!"

options.text: Who?
options.why: Even if you don't know them, you just ended it.

options.text: The reunion! Sixteen years apart, and then almost three million people came. Did the brothers behave?
options.why: Shows you know, adds the scale, and asks the question every fan loves.

options.text: Oasis sold almost three million tickets on the reunion tour, and it was their first tour since 2009.
options.why: Accurate, but it's your fact, not their story.

dropIn.pattern: Know it + ask the fan question

dropIn.fact: In March 2026 BTS released "Arirang", their first album since 2020, named after a famous Korean folk song. Their world tour began in April 2026.
dropIn.prompt: A Korean traveller at the hostel mentions she's a BTS fan.

options.text: I don't really like K-pop.
options.why: Nobody asked for your verdict.

options.text: BTS released an album called "Arirang" in 2026.
options.why: Right fact, no warmth.

options.text: Then this is your year — first BTS album since 2020, and they named it after "Arirang". Are you going to the tour?
options.why: Shares her excitement with a fact she'll love.

dropIn.fact: Nepathya is a folk-rock band from Pokhara, formed in 1990 and led by Amrit Gurung. They mix Nepali folk tunes with rock.
dropIn.prompt: A traveller asks, "What Nepali music should I listen to?"

options.text: Start with Nepathya — a folk-rock band from right here in Pokhara, playing since 1990. Put them on during a bus ride and count how many people sing along.
options.why: Local pride, a clear pick, and a fun test.

options.text: Nepali music is only for Nepali people.
options.why: Closes a door they wanted to open.

options.text: Nepathya is a band from Pokhara.
options.why: Correct, but it doesn't sell it.

dropIn.fact: Kutumba is a Nepali instrumental band, formed in 2004, that plays folk music on traditional instruments like the sarangi and the madal.
dropIn.prompt: A traveller who plays violin asks about traditional Nepali instruments.

options.text: We just use guitars now.
options.why: Not true, and a missed chance.

options.text: Look up Kutumba — an instrumental band that plays old Nepali instruments like the sarangi, which is a bit like your violin's village cousin.
options.why: A tip, a comparison to their own instrument, and a smile.

options.text: Kutumba plays traditional Nepali instruments.
options.why: Useful but flat.

dropIn.fact: George Harrison of the Beatles learned the sitar from Indian master Ravi Shankar, and it changed the sound of Beatles songs.
dropIn.prompt: In a Thamel shop, a traveller is holding a sitar, wondering if they should buy it.

options.text: You'll never learn it.
options.why: Discouraging and rude.

options.text: George Harrison learned the sitar from Ravi Shankar and it changed the Beatles' sound, so you never know where it could take you.
options.why: Encouraging, but a bit long and formal.

options.text: Careful — George Harrison picked one up and it changed the Beatles. This could be your start.
options.why: Short, inspiring and a little dramatic.

dropIn.fact: Coldplay formed in London in the 1990s, when the members were students at University College London.
dropIn.prompt: A traveller jokes, "Coldplay is just music for sad students."

options.text: Coldplay is terrible anyway.
options.why: Joins in by insulting — no fun, no wit.

options.text: Well, they did start as students in London. So you're not wrong — you're just early.
options.why: Agrees with a twist, using the fact.

options.text: Actually, Coldplay formed when the members were students at University College London in the 1990s.
options.why: The "actually" turns a joke into a correction.
